messages.subject: Re: EFA and CEFAPak
messages.subject_clean: EFA and CEFAPak
messages.body_plain:
Hi Elena,

the EFA features in lavaan are not yet document as we are still trying to figure out some rarely occurring estimation problems.

The EFAutilities package is a very fine package.

You can find an example how to use a target rotation here:
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/EFAutilities/EFAutilities.pdf
(p. 10)

Actually, it's a partial target rotation, that is, you don't have to guess all target values but instead you can tell it some values and say "estimate for the others whatever comes out".

Therefore, you have to specify targets and weights. A weight of 0 means ("Don't care about the value of this loading.").

I would try, to specify all cross-loadings to zero und only put weights on these. In an oblique case, you also need a target for the factor correlation matrix (but you can leave this open if you don't have any specific expectations such as orthogonality between certain factors).

What you could also try is a geomin rotation with an increased epsilon of say 0.5. This results in a rotation that can handle cross-loadings quite well. See, e.g., here: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/10705511.2018.1558060?needAccess=true (Disclaimer as this is my own paper: No, advertisement intended, there are other sources for this, this was just the quickest way to underline the idea.)

I would expect that some of your facets are highly correlated and that this results in a partially conflated solution. It is a well-established finding that some oblique rotations tend to produce such conflated solutions.

Lastly, I would like to remind you of being open to the possibility that the original factor model is wrong (or at least cannot hold for your data set). Therefore, I'd invite you to be transparent about the CFA result and just tell the reader about these problems.

First of all, if you have specific expectations, I would start with a CFA in which you put your theoretical model to a test. messages.body_plain:
> Could you please tell me whether my code for strong measurement invariance in the multilevel context (two-level) is correct?

You use the same labels for loadings at both levels, which implies metric invariance across levels (and by necessity across clusters because loadings cannot yet be random variables).  You also fix Level-2 residual variances to zero, which implies scalar invariance across clusters.  There cannot be scalar invariance across levels because all Level-1 intercepts are zero by definition.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Hi Group,

I have a 2-factor model with 8 items loading onto each factor, and the response scale ranges from 0-3 for each item. According to what I know, I should be using estimator = "WLSMV" and test = "mean.var.adjusted" due to the fact that my data is categorical (e.g., Finney and DiStefano, 2006).

  Comparative Fit Index (CFI)                    0.970       0.819

  Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI)                       0.965       0.789

Can someone help me with what's happening here? Is it due to the scaling correction factor, shift parameter, or something else? Which test statistic should I use / report? Or, more broadly, please correct me if I'm using the wrong estimator and/or test for my categorical data.

"Bugs/glitches discovered after the release:
the (new) robust CFI/TLI/RMSEA values as printed in the summary() output of version 0.5-21 (only) are wrong if (and only if) the test statistic is “mean.var.adjusted” or “scaled.shifted” (the latter is used when estimator = “WLSMV”, the default estimator in the categorical case)"

Thank you all for your help.

messages.body_plain:
> EVERY indicator in my model has cross-loading. In this case, does it still make sense to manually free any latent means?

Since you have a bifactor or MTMM model, constraining intercepts to equality only allows you to estimate differences in means of EITHER general / trait factors OR specific / method factors.  You could even fit both models to compare their fit (although I doubt they are nested; you could use net() to check).  I would recommend adding "means" to your group.equal= argument, which should avoid the error (since means will all be fixed to zero).  Then you can copy / paste or use update() to free only the (set of) means to specify the model you want to fit.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

No, you can't do that in lavaan.  Maybe using product indicators, but I've not seen that applied to growth models (which have fixed, not estimated loadings).

Hi Guido,

I am not sure if Lavaan has an argument for that. But I did have the same issue and this is what I've done:

residual_order<-resid(fit, "cor")$cov
cov_tibble <- tibble(variables = NA, cov = NA)
for (rowname in rownames(residual_order)) {
  for (colname in colnames(residual_order)) {
    cov_tibble %<>%
      rbind(
        tibble(variables = paste(rownames(residual_order)[which(rownames(residual_order) == rowname)],
                                 colnames(residual_order)[which(colnames(residual_order) == colname)]),
               cov = residual_order[rownames(residual_order)[which(rownames(residual_order) == rowname)],
                                    colnames(residual_order)[which(colnames(residual_order) == colname)]])
      )
  }
}
cov_tibble %<>% {.[-1, ]} %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(cov)))

You will find a new object called "cov_tibble" with the arranged values in descending order. Hope it helps :)

Fran

messages.subject: Re: Parallel growth model
messages.subject_clean: Parallel growth model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This can be done with the growth() function (which really just calls on the lavaan() function). This is not the same as multilevel sem.

for three time points, intercept and slope only, this would look like:

model <-
'
Intercept1 =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3
slope1 =~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3

Intercept2 =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3
slope2 =~ 0*y1 + 1*y2 + 2*y3

'

fit<- growth(model, data = dat)
summary(fit)

pay attention to your covariances if you have specific specifications (e.g., intercept predicting slope), but this will have all latent vars covary and have estimated variances by default.

Yes, latent variables automatically are given a variance and a covariance which you'll see.

If you want a significance test to see if the rate is significantly different (if that matters to you at all, it might not, but it sounds like this might be what you're doing), you'll have to be creative though.

In particular you'd want to specify a model which had no constraints on the slope (i.e., what I wrote above), then another model which constrains them to be the same, then you'd do a lavTestLRT(fit1, fit2) call on the two fitted objects. If the test is significant, then you'd prefer the model without the constraint, which would say the slopes are significantly different, otherwise they are not significantly different.

messages.body_plain:
Lets imagine I have the following data: 20 participants each rated 10 items on five different dimensions.

set.seed(123)
library(data.table)
library(psych)

ppt <- rep(1:20, each = 10)
item <- rep(1:10, times = 20)

dim_a <- rnorm(200)
dim_b <- rnorm(200)
dim_c <- rnorm(200)
dim_d <- rnorm(200)
dim_e <- rnorm(200)

d <- as.data.table(cbind(ppt, item, dim_a, dim_b, dim_c, dim_d, dim_e))

Lets say I'd like to conduct a CFA with dims a-c on one factor, and dims d-e on another. I believe I can do so with something like this.

twofactor <- ' f1 =~ dim_a + dim_b + dim_c
f2 =~ dim_d + dim_e '

fit <- cfa(twofactor, data = d)

However, I would like to account for the fact that ratings are nested in both participants and items. Is there a way to account for this? If I were running a regression the terminology would be that I would like to add a random intercept for participants and items.

It seems like I can do one by adding a cluster argument...

fit <- cfa(twofactor, data = d, cluster = "ppt")

But is it possible to do both participants and items? Note that participants and items are not nested but crossed.

messages.subject: Re: Simulating orthogonal responses in observed variable model
messages.subject_clean: Simulating orthogonal responses in observed variable model
messages.body_plain:
Hi.  I was not able to run your code, perhaps because I am using an older version.  So, I simulated the data manually.

The full data generating model has two treatment variables.  The outcomes are a stochastic functions of a latent treatment variable, call it TrtLV and the observed treatment variable, TrtObs is a determinate function of TrtLV based on the threshold model.  Of course the outcomes will be unconditionally dependent because they both depend upon TrtLV but I assume that what you meant was that you want them to be conditionally independent when you condition on treatment.

They should be conditionally independent conditional on TrtLV (confirmed in model 1).  However, the data only gives you TrtObs which contains less information than TrtLV.  As a result, conditioning on TrtObs does not suffice to produce conditional independence (confirmed in model 2).  However, if one can model TrtObs using a latent variable to represent TrtLV, then conditional independence is recovered (confirmed in model 3).

Here is my code:

# Data Simulation
Nobs = 10000 # Sample Size
TrtLV <- rnorm(Nobs, 0, 1) # Latent Treatment
Grazers1 <- (-1.5 * TrtLV) + rnorm(Nobs, 0, 1) # Outcome 1
Grazers2 <- (-0.8 * TrtLV) + rnorm(Nobs, 0, 1) # Outcome 2
TrtObs <- rep(0, times=Nobs) # Observed Treatment
TrtObs[TrtLV > 0] <- 1
Nada <- rnorm(Nobs, 0, 1) # Random instrument
myData <- data.frame(TrtLV, Grazers1, Grazers2, TrtObs, Nada) # Data frame
pairs(myData) # Scatterplot matrix

mod1 <- '
  Grazers1 ~ TrtLV
  Grazers2 ~ TrtLV
  TrtLV ~~ TrtLV
  Grazers1 ~~ Grazers1
  Grazers2 ~~ Grazers2
  Grazers1 ~~ Grazers2
' # end mod1

fit1 <- lavaan(model=mod1, data=myData)
summary(fit1) # Covariance between Grazers1 and Grazers 2 residuals not statistically significant

mod2 <- '
  Grazers1 ~ TrtObs
  Grazers2 ~ TrtObs
  TrtObs ~~ TrtObs
  Grazers1 ~~ Grazers1
  Grazers2 ~~ Grazers2
  Grazers1 ~~ Grazers2
' # end mod2

fit2 <- lavaan(model=mod2, data=myData)
summary(fit2) # Covariance between Grazers1 and Grazers 2 residuals statistically significant

mod3 <- '
  Grazers1 ~ TrtObs
  Grazers2 ~ TrtObs
  TrtObs ~ Nada
  TrtObs ~~ TrtObs
  TrtObs | t1
  Grazers1 ~~ Grazers1
  Grazers2 ~~ Grazers2
  Grazers1 ~~ Grazers2
  Grazers1 ~ 1
  Grazers2 ~ 1
' # end mod3

fit3 <- lavaan(model=mod3, data=myData, ordered=c("TrtObs"))
summary(fit3) # Covariance between Grazers1 and Grazers 2 residuals not statistically significant

I could not think of a way to tell lavaan to treat TrtObs as an endogenous variable off the top of my head.  So, I added Nada as a useless predictor to render TrtObs endogenous.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Yes, this is necessary in the version on CRAN.  If you install the development version <https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki>, I enabled a clumsy way to avoid needing raw data, using the sample.nobs= argument to specify an arbitrary vector whose length indicates the number of groups.

EN17.CFA <- '
EN.Need =~ EN.Personal.Need.6 + EN.Family.Need.15 + EN.Culture.Need.24
EN.Personal =~ EN.Personal.Loved1 + EN.Personal.Exp.2 + EN.Personal.Imp.5
EN.Culture =~ EN.Family.Enjoyed.10 + EN.Culture.Joy.23 + EN.Culture.Know.31
EN.Current =~ EN.Current.Personal.32 + EN.Current.Forward.35 +
              EN.Current.PosExp.38 + EN.Current.Meprobs.43
EN.Art =~ En.Art.ImgSnow.46 + En.Art.Imgflks.47 +
          EN.Art.PicLife.Snow.57 + EN.Art.PicLife.Play.58 +
          EN.Art.PicLife.Trav.59 + EN.Art.PicLife.Work.60
EN.AtAv =~ EN.AtAv.Intrig.63 + EN.AtAv.Awe.64 + EN.AtAv.Unsafe.67
EN.Famil =~ EN.Famil.Safe.79 + EN.Famil.Belong.83 + EN.Famil.Exper.86
'

EN17.gender.config <- measEq.syntax(EN17.CFA, group="Gender", sample.nobs=c(1,1),
                                    ID.fac="auto.fix.first", meanstructure=TRUE)
mod.config <- as.character(EN17.gender.config)
cat(mod.config) # there are now 2 values/labels per parameter

You could also do this with categorical data, but (if data= is missing) syntax would need to specify the correct number of thresholds.  If you are using lavaan to fit the model, there may not be any good reason to do it that way.  But as.character() is also intended to write Mplus syntax, in which case perhaps users don't want to fit models with lavaan.

messages.body_plain:
> Reaching out to see if anyone is aware of the existence of formal simulation paper comparing different ways to handle categorical data in lavaan.

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2017.1421467

Also ask on SEMNET, there are more people to respond (especially Cam MacIntosh, who is a living database of references)

https://listserv.ua.edu/cgi-bin/wa?SUBED1=semnet&A=1

> 2) using WLSMV without ordered = c()

That would not make sense.  The procedure is designed for categorical data.  Thresholds and polychoric correlations are estimated first, then the model is fitted to those.  The weight matrix is calculated from the uncertainty of the threshold and polychoric estimates.  If you don't estimate them, what weight matrix would you use?

> 3) using blavaan for bayesian

blavaan cannot yet handle categorical outcomes.  Ed is working on it, but the computation time is incredibly slow, so it might be a while until he can make a practical solution available.

> 4) using MLR

This one is specifically about testing invariance with missing ordinal data.  It includes a comparison of WLSMV with FIML(R)
https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2019.1608799

> 5) varying the number of levels (e.g., dichotomous vs. 3 level ordered vs. more levels etc.)

In the first paper I linked to, we had 2 or 5 categories.   The second only had 5 categories.  Rhemtulla et al. did a comprehensive simulation study comparing 2, 3, ... 7 categories (also MLR vs. WLSMV), but it was before lavaan could analyze categorical data, so I think she used Mplus or EQS.

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

In fact, there are many studies comparing WLSMV to MLR, but they typically use Mplus.  lavaan uses the same specifications as Mplus, so they should still be informative for you.

> Ideally datasets which would lead to significant and nonsignificant thresholds would be used, because I have heard discussion about the adequacy of not using ordered = c() when the thresholds are non-significant.

I don't know if you simply misunderstood, but a nonsignificant threshold does not mean your data are not categorical.  It just means the proportion of subjects above/below that threshold is not statistically distinguishable from 50/50%.  If you have a binary item with 50% in each category, your threshold will be exactly zero, and you should absolutely still declare it as ordered=.  If anything, you might consider fixing the threshold to zero instead of estimating it, but if that was not an a priori hypothesis, there is no good reason to do that just to avoid a nonsignificant threshold estimate.  The point of thresholds is not to be nonzero (they are not factor loadings).

messages.subject: Re: Can lavaan conduct a CFA or SEM with two crossed random effects?
messages.subject_clean: Can lavaan conduct a CFA or SEM with two crossed random effects?
messages.body_plain:
> Lets imagine I have the following data: 20 participants each rated 10 items on five different dimensions.

What makes the first item on Dimension 1 the "same" item as the first on Dimensions 2-5?

> I would like to account for the fact that ratings are nested in both participants and items. Is there a way to account for this?

CFA / SEM handles nesting of responses within items the same way it handles nesting of repeated measures within subjects in a latent growth model: by putting the different responses into wide format (dim_a_item1, dim_a_item2, etc.).  You would of course need a lot more subjects for a model with 5*10 = 50 variables, but that is just how CFA works.  The "nesting" issue then disappears because all responses for a subject are within a single row, and dependence among them is accounted for in the model's covariance structure.

In this case, you would want to read about bifactor or multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) models.  You would have a factor for each dimension ("trait factors"), and if the 10 items are indeed matched across dimensions (e.g., they use similar wordings or themes), then you would also have "method factors" (one factor onto which each "item1" loads, another onto which each "item2" loads, etc.).  Once the trait and method factors are all specified, then you can specify any higher-order factor structure you like among the 5 dimensions.  However, MTMM models are notorious for not converging, so good luck.

> If I were running a regression the terminology would be that I would like to add a random intercept for participants and items.
>
> It seems like I can do one by adding a cluster argument...
>
> fit <- cfa(twofactor, data = d, cluster = "ppt")
>
> But is it possible to do both participants and items?

No, lavaan can only handle a single cluster variable.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: ordered observable exogenous variables in path analysis
messages.subject_clean: ordered observable exogenous variables in path analysis
messages.body_plain:
> Of course, I can go around it and turn my factor variable into a sequence of dummy variables, and it works, but can lavaan accommodate ordered exogenous variables?

No, you need to use dummies:  https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

If you really want to interpret the effect of an underlying normally distributed latent response, you would have to treat it as a single-indicator factor:

mod <- ' x1 + x2 ~ AGE
AGE =~ ageyr
ageyr ~~ 0*ageyr
AGE ~~ 1*AGE
'
summary(sem(mod, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, ordered = "ageyr", parameterization = "theta"))

But that is highly dubious for "age".  Certainly age is actually continuous, but it is not normally distributed, and tends to be completely dependent on your sampling design.  So I would recommend treating your few categories as categories.   If it is measured in years, you could always test a linearity constraint using labels:

for (i in 12:16) HolzingerSwineford1939[,paste0("age", i)] <- as.integer(HolzingerSwineford1939$ageyr == i)
mod <- ' x1 ~ b1_12*age12 + b1_13*age13 + b1_14*age14 + b1_15*age15 + b1_16*age16
## year 11 is reference group, so first slope is a 1-year effect.
'
con <- '## constrain other years to be a multiple of it
b1_13 == 2*b1_12
b1_14 == 3*b1_12
b1_15 == 4*b1_12
b1_16 == 5*b1_12
'
fit <- sem(mod, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
lavTestWald(fit, constraints = con) # fail to reject H0 of linearity

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: categorical variables: lavaan and Mplus
messages.subject_clean: categorical variables: lavaan and Mplus
messages.body_plain:
> How can this approach be applied if the data is non-normal?

Categorical data are already not normal.  Do you mean the underlying latent item-response (LIR) is not normal?  You can generate a continuous LIR using any distribution you want (e.g., runif), but once data are discretized, lavaan could not know anything about the true distribution of the LIR.  It can only assume LIRs are normal.  If you are savvy enough to program your own likelihood functions, you could use OpenMx to specify alternative distributions of the LIR.

> The real data I am interested in analysing is actually very non-normal. In this case, is it appropriate to apply the constraints mean = 0 and var = 1

All continuous distributions have means and variances, and the same identification conditions would apply.  But again, lavaan is only capable of assuming normality of LIRs.

messages.subject_clean: possible to model piecewise growth modeling using lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan community,

I'm taking baby steps with learning how to conduct piecewise growth modeling and I wonder if this can be done using lavaan? I've read through a lavaan tutorial on latent growth curves  but I can't even begin how to imagine how to modify it to address my research questions.

Here is a brief summary of my data and my research questions:

I have about 300 students that are clustered in 48 classrooms or teachers that come from 4 school districts and their reading and mathematics achievement is tracked across 3 years.  Each student was tested 3 times (fall, winter, and spring) within each year, so they all have 9 data points across 3 years.  However, the testing times vary across students and schools, i.e., time-varying observations.  Plotting the individual growth curves shows that within each year, students' performance increases in a linear fashion, but there is a slight dip in performance at the beginning of year 2 compared to at the end of year 1, and at the beginning of year 3 compared to at the end of year 2.  Hence, I believe I should model their growth with 3 intercept growth factors and 3 slope growth factors. After that, I'm hoping to enter teacher level predictors hoping to account for some of the variation in students' growth.

If you have a piecewise growth model syntax sample out there that you're willing to share, that would be really great but any guidance would be wonderful.  Also, after having examined some examples in papers and in forums, I'm still scratching my head about how to specify time scores because I've seen people specify them very differently, but there's very little explanation of why they specified them that way.  In my example, I'm guessing that it's like this.  Could someone please confirm whether I'm on the right track?
0 1 2                        (time scores piece 1)
         0 1 2               (time scores piece 2)
                  0 1 2       (time scores piece 3)

0 1 2 because I'm assuming that the growth is linear.  However, do these time scores assume that there's equal spacing between time 1, time 2, and time 3? If so, my data won't meet this assumption because students get tested at different times within a single testing period (i.e., fall, winter, spring).

Thank you for your kind attention on this and for any input you can provide.

messages.subject: Re: LGCM- model did not converge error
messages.subject_clean: LGCM- model did not converge error
messages.body_plain:
Your data does not reflect the model you imposed, yes.

You can try to assess the construct over time in ggplot (or base R) to see if the data looks to be linearly increasing over time. You don't have enough data points to try higher orders of fit, but it's possible one/both of these only has a significant intercept term (i.e., doesn't increase over time). If that is the case, you could have an intercept-only (for one construct) and intercept and slope, instead of the PPM you presented.

Get fit for just 1 latent growth curve first, and if it fits well, put it with the other latent growth curve. (These estimates are not trustable, but best guess suggests s2 with a near 0 intercept and variance might be causing the trouble.)

I don't think this will help with convergence, but you might want to look into grouping your large data file (dat) into just the young and old groups and making a grouping variable, then following the instructions here (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html).

For example:

library(tidyverse)
small_dat<-dat %>% filter(age < ## | age > ##)

small_dat$Group <- ifelse(small_dat$age < ##, "Young", "Old")

Then call the Lavaan object

fit <- growth(model, data = small_dat, group = "Group")

and when you call summary(fit), you'll get both group's results.

Hope this helps,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Parallel growth model
messages.subject_clean: Parallel growth model
messages.body_plain:
You're close, you constrained them to be the same, but also constrained them to be 0, which you don't want if I'm understanding you correctly. That is a good model to compare intercept-only to intercept and slope growth.

If you're specifically looking to test if the two slopes are significantly different from one another (or technically, if the model fits significantly better when they're specified separately or not), you will do the unconstrained PPM like above, then the constrained PPM.

You'll want to set the slopes to be equal with a label (both the same label), like this:

constrainedMod <-

'
Intercept1 =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3
slope1 =~ 0*x1 + 1*x2 + 2*x3

Intercept2 =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3
slope2 =~ 0*y1 + 1*y2 + 2*y3

s1~constraint*1
s2~constraint*1

'
then do an lavTestLRT(unconstrainedMod, constrainedMod). The null hypothesis of this test is essentially that the models fit the same, if so, pick the one with more df because its parsimonious.

Regarding fit measures, there's an entire literature on this. Hu & Bentler 1999 is often cited, but there are papers about how incremental fit indices are poorer for growth curves. In my own work, I typically have had growth curves fit the Hu & Bentler criteria, though. The importance of fit is related to how important accurate interpretations are. Fit tells you if the model you impose is reflected in the data.

Freed timepoints can be compared to fixed timepoints with lavTestLRT() as well. Models can be more complex that way and you will need some SEM knowlegde to interpret correctly, but if you have more than 3 waves of data it's possible.

Explore this youtube channel for theoretical understanding of some of your questions: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7kcXN1Xoj4PzMIKPHJ5m7Q/videos

messages.body_plain:
May,
Better still, let me explain how you can answer such questions in the future.  Here is the line of code in question.

data <- as.data.frame(matrix(sample(c(1:5,99),100, replace = TRUE),20,5))

The first thing to notice is that this is an assignment, so we can ignore the "data <-" and focus on parsing the right hand side which would be a valid line of code evaluating an expression all by itself.

Next, notice that the expression is formed by nesting the following functions:
as.data.frame()
matrix()
sample()
c()

So, the next thing you want to do is to look at the help files for each of these functions to learn their parameters.
?as.data.frame
?matrix
?sample
?c

Now we can work our way through step by step in order.  I will work from the inside out.

c(1:5, 99)

The colon is shorthand for seq(from=1, to=5, by=1).  So, the result is the vector 1,2,3,4,5,99.  To simplify notaton and break down the steps, let's call that Ralph.

Ralph <- c(1:5, 99)
sample(Ralph,100, replace = TRUE)

According to the help file, the first two parameters to sample() are x and size.  So, a sample is being drawn from Ralph of size 100.  Let's name the parameters and call this Alice.

Alice <- sample(x = Ralph, size = 100, replace = TRUE)
matrix(Alice,20,5)

The first three parameters to the matrix() function  are data, nrow, and ncol.  So, this is taking the data from Alice and arranging it in a matrix with 20 rows and 5 columns.  Let's call that Trixie.

Trixie <- matrix(data=Alice, nrow=20, ncol=5)
as.data.frame(Trixie)

The first parameter to as.data.frame is x, the object to be converted to a data frame.

as.data.frame(x = Trixie)

HTH,

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

On Friday, June 26, 2020 at 7:18:40 AM UTC-7, Nickname wrote:
> May,
> Better still, let me explain how you can answer such questions in the future.  Here is the line of code in question.
>
> data <- as.data.frame(matrix(sample(c(1:5,99),100, replace = TRUE),20,5))
>
> The first thing to notice is that this is an assignment, so we can ignore the "data <-" and focus on parsing the right hand side which would be a valid line of code evaluating an expression all by itself.
>
> Next, notice that the expression is formed by nesting the following functions:
> as.data.frame()
> matrix()
> sample()
> c()
>
> So, the next thing you want to do is to look at the help files for each of these functions to learn their parameters.
> ?as.data.frame
> ?matrix
> ?sample
> ?c
>
> Now we can work our way through step by step in order.  I will work from the inside out.
>
> c(1:5, 99)
>
> The colon is shorthand for seq(from=1, to=5, by=1).  So, the result is the vector 1,2,3,4,5,99.  To simplify notaton and break down the steps, let's call that Ralph.
>
> Ralph <- c(1:5, 99)
> sample(Ralph,100, replace = TRUE)
>
> According to the help file, the first two parameters to sample() are x and size.  So, a sample is being drawn from Ralph of size 100.  Let's name the parameters and call this Alice.
>
> Alice <- sample(x = Ralph, size = 100, replace = TRUE)
> matrix(Alice,20,5)
>
> The first three parameters to the matrix() function  are data, nrow, and ncol.  So, this is taking the data from Alice and arranging it in a matrix with 20 rows and 5 columns.  Let's call that Trixie.
>
> Trixie <- matrix(data=Alice, nrow=20, ncol=5)
> as.data.frame(Trixie)
>
> The first parameter to as.data.frame is x, the object to be converted to a data frame.
>
> as.data.frame(x = Trixie)
>
> HTH,
> Keith
> ------------------------
> Keith A. Markus
> John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
> Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.

messages.subject: Bootstrapping (BCa) doesn't work
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapping (BCa) doesn't work
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to run a mediation analysis within a cross-lagged model (i.e., trying to see if another factor mediates one of the significant cross-lagged paths).
However, when I try to run bootstrapping (BCa) and to get 90% CIs, I am getting a warning and an error message, so I don't think it worked.

Warning message:
In norm.inter(t, adj.alpha) : extreme order statistics used as endpoints

Error in object.size(obj) : could not find function "object.size"

I've read somewhere that getting this warning message may mean that it's better to use another test because for small datasets, the interval from BCa may be wider than for some other methods. Can anyone please share with me the syntax for other bootstrapping methods which may be appropriate in this case?
I am including my syntax below for reference.

Thank you so much!

May

## Testing mediation within a two-wave cross-lagged model

mod2ms<-'

#regressions

smanx_c1~chsex_d1+cage_d1
smanx_m1~chsex_d1+cage_d1
smanx_m2~smanx_m1+smanx_c1+cage_d2

## direct effect (c’ designated as c here), path b1:
smanx_c2 ~ c*smanx_m1 + b1*MSupES + b2*smanx_c1 + b3*cage_d2

##path a1
MSupES ~ a1*smanx_m1

#covariance
smanx_c1~~smanx_m1
smanx_c2~~smanx_m2
cage_d1~~cage_d2
chsex_d1~~cage_d1+cage_d2

#variance
smanx_c1~~smanx_c1
smanx_c2~~smanx_c2
smanx_m1~~smanx_m1
smanx_m2~~smanx_m2
chsex_d1~~chsex_d1
cage_d1~~cage_d1
cage_d2~~cage_d2
MSupES~~MSupES

#intercept
smanx_c1~1
smanx_c2~1
smanx_m1~1
smanx_m2~1
chsex_d1~1
cage_d1~1
cage_d2~1
MSupES~1

### Test Indirect Effects
Indirectfx := a1*b1

### get total effect (c)
Total := c + (a1*b1)

'

fit2ms=lavaan(mod2ms, data=depanx, se = 'bootstrap', bootstrap=1000L, fixed.x=FALSE, auto.var = TRUE, meanstructure=TRUE, missing= 'FIML')

summary(fit2ms, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE, rsq=TRUE)

fitMeasures(fit2ms, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "rmsea", "cfi", "tli","nfi" ,"srmr"))

## To get rmsea 90% CIs

fitMeasures(fit2ms)
boot.fit2ms <- parameterEstimates(fit2ms, boot.ci.type="bca.simple")
boot.fit2ms

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapping (BCa) doesn't work
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapping (BCa) doesn't work
messages.body_plain:
I don't think you can calculate a true BCa confidence interval with lavaan. As far as I know, bca.simple <http://bca.simple> does not correct for acceleration. However, you can use the boot package if that is important to you. You may be able to get rid of the warning message if you increase the number of bootstraps significantly. You do not need another bootrap method. You only need to change boot.ci.type <http://boot.ci.type> to request other ci types:
https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/lavaan/versions/0.6-6/topics/parameterEstimates
However, whether this procedure makes sense for fit coefficients like the RMSEA is another question:
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124192021002004

Hello,

I've posted here before, but am still having a bit of trouble with some errors in my code.

My model is below (N=1282, number of free parameters = 141):

#install.packages("lavaan") #for SEM
library(lavaan)

mymodel <- '

rEP =~ sresilience_q3 +  sresilience_q6 + sresilience_q7 + sresilience_q11 + sresilience_q13 + sresilience_q15 + sresilience_q16 + sresilience_q17 + sresilience_q21 + sresilience_q22

bur =~ inq_q1 + inq_q2 + inq_q3 + inq_q4 + inq_q5

belonging =~ inq_q6r + inq_q7r + inq_q8 + inq_q9 + inq_q10r

dep =~ cessds_q1 + cessds_q2 + cessds_q3 + cessds_q4 + cessds_q5r + cessds_q6 + cessds_q7 + cessds_q8r + cessds_q9 + cessds_q10

#structural model

def ~ dep

ent ~ def + dep

idea ~  ent + bur + bel + rEP + rES + rIP + dep'

# model identification and estimation
modelfit <- sem(mymodel, data = mydatat1, estimator = "MLM")

summary(modelfit_ideation, fit.measures = T, standardized = T, rsquare = T)

I get two errors in my output:

1. lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative

I should note that the model above is a direct replication study of a published SEM in MPlus (but using a different sample). My current understanding is that this error may be a result of a misspecified model, but I can't say for sure.

and

2. When I try to print the R square values for my latent variables, I get NA for one of them.

These errors don't happen when I include a different outcome variable that is binary ('ordered') and specify my model estimation as DWLS.

In the output, I also seem to get two columns worth of values (e.g. fo CFI and TLI), and I can't seem to find guidance as to which one to take note of:

I'm quite new to this, and I'd really appreciate some guidance on these errors, and what I could be doing wrong.

Many thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Ros,

I might be able to help a little.

For point 1, check the residual variances section. I'm betting you'll find that "ent" is the latent with the negative residual. That would explain point 2, because the R^2 is undefined (or could be reported as >1, also unallowable) if more variance in ent is accounted for than exists.

For point 3, you requested MLM in your sem() call, which is the Satorra-Bentler adjusted ("robust") chi-square. Since you asked for the robust statistic, I would think that's the column you want to look at for chi-square and statistics based on it e..g., CFI), even though lavaan returns the unadjusted/standard as well.

Pat

Hi All,

This may seem similar to other issues. I have read up on https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/lavaan/SYTgS8EfnLg/13aIN8xoAQAJ but didn't seem to help so I decided to make a new post. My model is the following:

Model = CSW =~ x1:x7
              LED =~ x8:x14
              GF =~ x14: x21
              VAN =~ x22:x28
              HN=~ x29:x33
              GN =~ a*VAN + a*LED
              VN =~ CSW + GF + HN

When I run this model I get the error stating some of the estimated latent variances are negative and it is for the factor VAN. So I fixed the error variance to equal to 0.01 and found the factor loads onto GN at 0.99. I then tried with GN and VN not being correlated and found the loading to decrease to 0.948. Normally, GN and VN correlate at around 0.4-0.5.

I also tried running LED and VAN as one factor but ended up with really poor model fit indices. When I run just the part of the model that involves GN I get a loading of 0.87 for VAN onto GN. I am not super familiar with the mathematics of this so I don't really understand what is going on. I thought maybe it was due to items from LED/VAN that were also loading highly onto the other factor, but modification indices quickly showed that was not the case. Currently, my next option is to explore model building to see where this issue might lie. But before I launch into that I wanted to see if you guys had any ideas.

For more contextual information LED only really correlates with VAN and none of the other factors (expected theoretically). The two LED and VAN factors make theoretical and we would expect to observe those.

My questions with this are:
Is it a problem to have a factor load at > 0.80 onto a second order factor, when there are only two manifest factors?
What are options around this error?
I really appreciate any feedback! Thank you
Danu

messages.subject: Re: Is data of 5 points likert scale exogenous?
messages.subject_clean: Is data of 5 points likert scale exogenous?
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure I understand your question. Any variable that is part of your model, is endogenous.  An exogenous variable is one outside the model (e.g. gender). This has nothing to do with Likert or if you are able to control the item responses. In your example you have an example question q12. I assume this is an item in your model (endogenous, dependent variable) which is influenced by the latent trait.
The reason for declaring variables ordered is to make sure they are not treated as continuous variables and that the polychoric correlation matrix is used for the calculations.
Again, please read https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html under 'categorical data'
cheers, G

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am fairly new to SEM and seeking some advice. I am running a SEM using the lavaan package to do mediation analysis and repeating the process on multiple imputed datasets. I have five latent variables (each made up of a number of ordered factor items), an exposure, and an outcome. I am using the latent variables as my mediators. I am interested in the direct and indirect effects. The estimator used was DWLS and I have a sample size of ~ 3,000. Each time I run the SEM (either with all five latent variables or with one latent variable) I get a number of warning messages as detailed below. Note that “my outcome variable”, “one of the items used for the latent variables” and “different item used for the latent variables” below are the variables that I am interested in.

In lav_bvmix_cor_twostep_fit(fit.y1 = UNI[[i]], fit.y2 = UNI[[j]],  :

  lavaan WARNING: estimation polyserial correlation did not converge for

                    variables [my outcome variable] and [one of the items used for the latent variables]

In lav_bvmix_cor_twostep_fit(fit.y1 = UNI[[i]], fit.y2 = UNI[[j]],  :

  lavaan WARNING: estimation polyserial correlation did not converge for

                    variables [my outcome variable] and [different item used for the latent variables]

etc.

The warning message above (i.e. “estimation polyserial correlation did not converge”) is only raised for a subset of my items making up the different latent variables and the outcome.

I should note that my models do converge even with these warning estimates and seem to provide sensible estimates. I would just like to understand what is causing these warnings and if I need to be concerned and/or address them.

Please could someone advice whether:
Do these warnings would affect the estimates?
Is it ok to use the estimates with these warnings?
A possible solution to these warning messages?

Many thanks

Kirsty

Cheers,
Brit

Michael

messages.body_plain:
> Dummy coding doesn't hold order information

No, but it doesn't have to.  It is less restrictive, so you can specify constraints that imply order, then test them against the less constrained model that uses dummy codes (e.g., you could specify a linear contrast among labeled parameters and pass those constraints to the lavTestWald() function).

> con <-'
> b11 < b12
> b12 < b13
>
> b21 < b22
> b22 < b23
>
> b31 < b32
> b32 < b33
>
> b41 < b42
> b42 < b43
> '

Since these are inequality constraints, you might find lavaan's InformativeTesting() function helpful.

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

It is less restrictive, so you can specify constraints that imply order, then test them against the less constrained model that uses dummy codes (e.g., you could specify a linear contrast among labeled parameters and pass those constraints to the lavTestWald() function).

> Since these are inequality constraints, you might find lavaan's InformativeTesting() function helpful.
